questions.topic: Calculus: Derivatives, Increasing/Decreasing Functions, Maxima and Minima
questions.sub_topic: Least cost of an open tank of fixed volume
questions.question: An open tank with a rectangular base is 2 m deep and holds 8 m³. Building the base costs ₹70 per m² and the sides ₹45 per m². The least cost of the tank is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) ₹1,000
Given: base \(x \times y\) with \(2xy = 8\), so \(xy = 4\); base cost \(70 \times 4 = ₹280\)
Formula: sides area \(= 2 \times 2(x + y) = 4\left(x + \dfrac{4}{x}\right)\); cost \(= 280 + 180\left(x + \dfrac{4}{x}\right)\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(x + \dfrac{4}{x}\right) = 1 - \dfrac{4}{x^2} = 0 \Rightarrow x = 2\) (a minimum)
Step 2: Cost \(= 280 + 180 \times 4 = ₹1{,}000\)
Common mistake: ₹1,180 (A) tries \(x = 1\). ₹720 (B) leaves out the base.
Key point: A square base gives the least side area for a fixed base area.

questions.sub_topic: Particular solution of (1 + e^(2x))dy + (1 + y²)eˣdx = 0
questions.question: The solution of \((1 + e^{2x})\,dy + (1 + y^2)e^x\,dx = 0\) with \(y(0) = 1\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(\tan^{-1}y + \tan^{-1}e^x = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\)
Given: \(\dfrac{dy}{1 + y^2} + \dfrac{e^x\,dx}{1 + e^{2x}} = 0\)
Formula: \(\tan^{-1}y + \tan^{-1}e^x = C\)
Step 1: \(y(0) = 1\): \(\dfrac{\pi}{4} + \dfrac{\pi}{4} = C\)
Step 2: \(C = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\)
Common mistake: (B) uses only one of the two \(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\) terms when finding \(C\).
Key point: With \(t = e^x\), \(\int\dfrac{e^x\,dx}{1 + e^{2x}} = \tan^{-1}e^x\).

questions.sub_topic: Maximum of 3x + 5y with two constraints
questions.question: The maximum value of \(Z = 3x + 5y\) subject to \(x + 3y \le 15\), \(x + y \le 7\), \(x, y \ge 0\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(29\)
Given: corners \((0, 0)\), \((7, 0)\), \((3, 4)\), \((0, 5)\)
Formula: evaluate \(Z\) at each corner
Step 1: \(Z = 0, 21, 29, 25\)
Step 2: The maximum is 29, at \((3, 4)\)
Common mistake: \(35\) (D) uses \((0, 7)\), which breaks \(x + 3y \le 15\).
Key point: Solve \(x + 3y = 15\), \(x + y = 7\) to get \((3, 4)\).

questions.topic: Algebra: Matrices, Determinants, Inverse and the Matrix Method
questions.sub_topic: Unknown entries from a matrix sum
questions.question: If \(\begin{bmatrix}x&3\\2&y\end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix}1&-1\\0&2\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}4&2\\2&5\end{bmatrix}\), then \(x + y\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(6\)
Given: equal matrices have equal entries
Formula: \(x + 1 = 4\), \(y + 2 = 5\)
Step 1: \(x = 3\), \(y = 3\); \(x + y = 6\)
Common mistake: \(9\) (B) adds 4 and 5 without subtracting.
Key point: Compare corresponding entries.

questions.topic: Algebra: Matrices, Determinants, Inverse and the Matrix Method
questions.sub_topic: A plus its inverse for a determinant-1 matrix
questions.question: For \(A = \begin{bmatrix}3&2\\4&3\end{bmatrix}\), the matrix \(A + A^{-1}\) equals:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(6I\)
Given: \(|A| = 9 - 8 = 1\)
Formula: \(A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix}3&-2\\-4&3\end{bmatrix}\)
Step 1: \(A + A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix}6&0\\0&6\end{bmatrix} = 6I\)
Common mistake: (C) is \(2A\), from taking \(A^{-1} = A\). (D) takes \(A^{-1} = -A\).
Key point: For a 2 × 2 matrix with determinant 1, the inverse just swaps the diagonal and changes two signs.

questions.topic: Algebra: Matrices, Determinants, Inverse and the Matrix Method
questions.sub_topic: Determinant when AᵀA = 4I for order 3
questions.question: \(A\) is a square matrix of order 3 with \(A^TA = 4I\). Then \(|A|\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(\pm 8\)
Given: \(|A^TA| = |A^T||A| = |A|^2\)
Formula: \(|4I_3| = 4^3 = 64\)
Step 1: \(|A|^2 = 64\)
Step 2: \(|A| = \pm 8\)
Common mistake: \(4\) (B) takes \(|4I| = 4\). (A) forgets the negative root.
Key point: \(|kI_n| = k^n\).

questions.sub_topic: The larger of two numbers drawn from 1, 2, 3 — which claims fail
questions.question:
Two different numbers are drawn at random from \(\{1, 2, 3\}\), and \(X\) is the larger of the two. Consider the following statements:
(A) \(P(X = 1) = 0\)
(B) \(E(X) = \dfrac{8}{3}\)
(C) \(\text{Var}(X) = \dfrac{4}{9}\)
(D) \(P(X = 3) = \dfrac{2}{3}\)
Which of the statements given above is/are NOT correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (C) only
Why: The pairs \(\{1, 2\}, \{1, 3\}, \{2, 3\}\) give \(X = 2, 3, 3\). So \(P(X = 2) = \dfrac{1}{3}\), \(P(X = 3) = \dfrac{2}{3}\), \(E(X) = \dfrac{8}{3}\). Only (C) is false: \(E(X^2) = \dfrac{4}{3} + 6 = \dfrac{22}{3}\), so \(\text{Var}(X) = \dfrac{22}{3} - \dfrac{64}{9} = \dfrac{2}{9}\).
Why not the others: (A) 1 is never the larger number. Options (A), (B) and (D) name a true statement as false.
Key point: List the outcomes before building the distribution.

questions.sub_topic: Area of the circle x² + y² = 4 beyond the line x + y = 2
questions.question: The area of the smaller region cut off from the circle \(x^2 + y^2 = 4\) by the line \(x + y = 2\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(\pi - 2\)
Given: the line meets the circle at \((2, 0)\) and \((0, 2)\)
Formula: area \(= \displaystyle\int_0^2\left(\sqrt{4 - x^2} - (2 - x)\right)dx\)
Step 1: \(\int_0^2\sqrt{4 - x^2}\,dx = \pi\) (a quarter circle of radius 2)
Step 2: \(\int_0^2(2 - x)\,dx = 2\); area \(= \pi - 2\)
Common mistake: \(\pi\) (A) forgets to subtract the triangle.
Key point: Area between curves = upper minus lower.

questions.topic: Calculus: Derivatives, Increasing/Decreasing Functions, Maxima and Minima
questions.sub_topic: Second derivative of e^(−x²) at 0
questions.question: If \(y = e^{-x^2}\), then \(\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}\) at \(x = 0\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(-2\)
Given: \(y' = -2xe^{-x^2}\)
Formula: \(y'' = -2e^{-x^2} + 4x^2e^{-x^2}\)
Step 1: At \(x = 0\): \(-2 + 0 = -2\)
Common mistake: \(0\) (A) evaluates \(y'\) instead. \(2\) (B) loses the minus sign.
Key point: Use the product rule on \(-2x \cdot e^{-x^2}\).

questions.topic: Calculus: Derivatives, Increasing/Decreasing Functions, Maxima and Minima
questions.sub_topic: Extreme values of x³ − 3x + 2
questions.question:
For \(f(x) = x^3 - 3x + 2\), match List-I with List-II.

List-I
(A) The local maximum value
(B) The local minimum value
(C) \(f''(2)\)
(D) The absolute maximum value on \([0, 3]\)

List-II
(I) \(0\)
(II) \(20\)
(III) \(12\)
(IV) \(4\)
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A)-(IV), (B)-(I), (C)-(III), (D)-(II)
Step 1: \(f'(x) = 3x^2 - 3 = 0\) at \(x = \pm 1\); \(f''(x) = 6x\)
Step 2: \(x = -1\): \(f'' < 0\), local maximum \(f(-1) = -1 + 3 + 2 = 4\) (IV)
Step 3: \(x = 1\): local minimum \(f(1) = 0\) (I); \(f''(2) = 12\) (III)
Step 4: On \([0, 3]\): \(f(0) = 2\), \(f(1) = 0\), \(f(3) = 27 - 9 + 2 = 20\) (II)
Common mistake: Giving the local maximum 4 as the answer to (D); on \([0, 3]\) the end point \(x = 3\) gives more.
Key point: An absolute maximum on a closed interval may be at an end point.

questions.sub_topic: At least two defectives in a draw of three
questions.question: A box has 5 good and 3 defective items. Three items are drawn at random without replacement, and \(X\) is the number of defectives drawn. \(P(X \ge 2)\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(\dfrac{2}{7}\)
Given: \(\binom{8}{3} = 56\) equally likely draws
Formula: \(P(X = 2) = \dfrac{\binom{3}{2}\binom{5}{1}}{56}\), \(P(X = 3) = \dfrac{\binom{3}{3}}{56}\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{15}{56} + \dfrac{1}{56} = \dfrac{16}{56}\)
Step 2: \(= \dfrac{2}{7}\)
Common mistake: \(\dfrac{15}{56}\) (A) counts only \(X = 2\). \(\dfrac{9}{8}\) (C) is \(E(X)\), not a probability.
Key point: "At least two" means two or three.

questions.sub_topic: Definite integral of x(1 − x)⁵ using a property
questions.question: \(\displaystyle\int_0^1 x(1 - x)^5\,dx\) equals:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(\dfrac{1}{42}\)
Given: \(\int_0^a f(x)\,dx = \int_0^a f(a - x)\,dx\)
Formula: \(\int_0^1 x(1 - x)^5\,dx = \int_0^1(1 - x)x^5\,dx\)
Step 1: \(\int_0^1(x^5 - x^6)\,dx = \dfrac{1}{6} - \dfrac{1}{7}\)
Step 2: \(= \dfrac{1}{42}\)
Common mistake: \(\dfrac{1}{6}\) (B) keeps only the first term.
Key point: The property turns a hard power into an easy one.

questions.topic: Algebra: Matrices, Determinants, Inverse and the Matrix Method
questions.sub_topic: Determinant of the adjoint of 3A⁻¹
questions.question: \(A\) is a square matrix of order 3 with \(|A| = 2\). Then \(|\text{adj}(3A^{-1})|\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(\dfrac{729}{4}\)
Given: \(n = 3\), \(|A^{-1}| = \dfrac{1}{2}\)
Formula: \(|\text{adj}\,M| = |M|^{n-1}\) and \(|kM| = k^n|M|\)
Step 1: \(|3A^{-1}| = 27 \times \dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{27}{2}\)
Step 2: \(|\text{adj}(3A^{-1})| = \left(\dfrac{27}{2}\right)^2 = \dfrac{729}{4}\)
Common mistake: \(\dfrac{27}{2}\) (A) stops at \(|3A^{-1}|\). \(729\) (D) forgets the factor \(|A^{-1}| = \dfrac{1}{2}\) and squares 27.
Key point: Work from the inside out: scalar, inverse, then adjoint.

questions.sub_topic: Separable equation y′ = y cot x through (π/2, 2)
questions.question: The solution of \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = y\cot x\) with \(y\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) = 2\) gives \(y\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)\) equal to:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(1\)
Given: \(\dfrac{dy}{y} = \cot x\,dx\)
Formula: \(\log|y| = \log|\sin x| + c\), so \(y = C\sin x\)
Step 1: \(2 = C\sin\dfrac{\pi}{2}\), so \(C = 2\)
Step 2: \(y\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) = 2 \times \dfrac{1}{2} = 1\)
Common mistake: \(\sqrt{3}\) (C) uses \(\cos\) instead of \(\sin\). \(\dfrac{1}{2}\) (D) forgets \(C = 2\).
Key point: \(\int\cot x\,dx = \log|\sin x|\).

questions.sub_topic: Four definite integrals — which hold
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) \(\displaystyle\int_{-1}^{1}x|x|\,dx = 0\)
(B) \(\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi}\sin^2 x\,dx = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\)
(C) \(\displaystyle\int_0^2[x]\,dx = 1\), where \([x]\) is the greatest integer not exceeding \(x\)
(D) \(\displaystyle\int_0^1 e^x\,dx = e\)
Which of the statements given above are correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: (A) \(x|x|\) is odd. (B) \(\sin^2 x = \dfrac{1 - \cos 2x}{2}\) gives \(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\). (C) \([x] = 0\) on \([0, 1)\) and \(1\) on \([1, 2)\), so the integral is \(0 + 1 = 1\).
Why not the others: (D) is false: \(\int_0^1 e^x\,dx = e - 1\). Options (C) and (D) include (D); (B) leaves out (C).
Key point: Split a greatest-integer integral at the integers.

questions.sub_topic: Partial fractions for 1/(x(x² + 1))
questions.question: \(\displaystyle\int\dfrac{dx}{x(x^2 + 1)}\) equals:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(\log|x| - \dfrac{1}{2}\log(x^2 + 1) + C\)
Given: \(\dfrac{1}{x(x^2 + 1)} = \dfrac{1}{x} - \dfrac{x}{x^2 + 1}\)
Formula: \(\int\dfrac{x}{x^2 + 1}\,dx = \dfrac{1}{2}\log(x^2 + 1)\)
Step 1: \(\log|x| - \dfrac{1}{2}\log(x^2 + 1) + C\)
Common mistake: (C) uses \(\dfrac{1}{x^2 + 1}\) instead of \(\dfrac{x}{x^2 + 1}\) for the second fraction.
Key point: A quadratic factor takes a numerator \(Bx + C\).

questions.sub_topic: Continuity and differentiability of four functions — which hold
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) \([x]\) (greatest integer) is continuous at \(x = 1.5\).
(B) \(|\sin x|\) is not differentiable at \(x = \pi\).
(C) \(e^{|x|}\) is differentiable at \(x = 0\).
(D) \(x^{1/3}\) is continuous at \(x = 0\).
Which of the statements given above are correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A), (B) and (D) only
Why: (A) \([x] = 1\) near 1.5. (B) \(\sin x\) changes sign at \(\pi\), so \(|\sin x|\) has a corner there (slopes \(-1\) and \(+1\)). (D) \(x^{1/3} \to 0\) as \(x \to 0\).
Why not the others: (C) is false: the left and right derivatives of \(e^{|x|}\) at 0 are \(-1\) and \(+1\). Options (C) and (D) include (C); (B) leaves out (D).
Key point: A modulus creates a corner where its inside changes sign.

questions.sub_topic: Condition from a determinant with 1 + x³ in a column
questions.question: \(x\), \(y\), \(z\) are distinct and \(\begin{vmatrix}x&x^2&1 + x^3\\y&y^2&1 + y^3\\z&z^2&1 + z^3\end{vmatrix} = 0\). Then \(xyz\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(-1\)
Given: split the third column: \(\begin{vmatrix}x&x^2&1\\\vdots\end{vmatrix} + \begin{vmatrix}x&x^2&x^3\\\vdots\end{vmatrix}\)
Formula: take \(xyz\) out of the second determinant; both reduce to \(\begin{vmatrix}1&x&x^2\\1&y&y^2\\1&z&z^2\end{vmatrix} = (x - y)(y - z)(z - x)\)
Step 1: The total is \((1 + xyz)(x - y)(y - z)(z - x)\)
Step 2: Distinct values make the product of differences non-zero, so \(1 + xyz = 0\) and \(xyz = -1\)
Common mistake: \(1\) (A) loses the sign. \(0\) (C) assumes one of the variables is 0.
Key point: Splitting a column turns one determinant into two.

questions.sub_topic: Point dividing a segment externally
questions.question: The position vector of the point dividing the join of \(A(1, 2, 3)\) and \(B(3, 4, 5)\) externally in the ratio \(2 : 1\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \((5, 6, 7)\)
Given: \(m = 2\), \(n = 1\)
Formula: external division: \(\dfrac{m\vec{b} - n\vec{a}}{m - n}\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{2(3, 4, 5) - (1, 2, 3)}{1} = (5, 6, 7)\)
Common mistake: (A) divides internally. (D) is the midpoint.
Key point: External division uses a minus sign.

questions.sub_topic: Value of p making two lines perpendicular
questions.question: The lines \(\dfrac{1 - x}{3} = \dfrac{7y - 14}{2p} = \dfrac{z - 3}{2}\) and \(\dfrac{7 - 7x}{3p} = \dfrac{y - 5}{1} = \dfrac{6 - z}{5}\) are perpendicular when \(p\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(\dfrac{70}{11}\)
Given: standard forms: \(\dfrac{x - 1}{-3} = \dfrac{y - 2}{2p/7} = \dfrac{z - 3}{2}\) and \(\dfrac{x - 1}{-3p/7} = \dfrac{y - 5}{1} = \dfrac{z - 6}{-5}\)
Formula: \(a_1a_2 + b_1b_2 + c_1c_2 = 0\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{9p}{7} + \dfrac{2p}{7} - 10 = 0\)
Step 2: \(\dfrac{11p}{7} = 10 \Rightarrow p = \dfrac{70}{11}\)
Common mistake: (D) keeps \(1 - x\) as if the ratio for \(x\) were \(+3\).
Key point: Make the coefficients of \(x\), \(y\), \(z\) equal to 1 before reading direction ratios.

questions.sub_topic: Derivative of √(x² + 1)
questions.question: \(\dfrac{d}{dx}\sqrt{x^2 + 1}\) equals:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(\dfrac{x}{\sqrt{x^2 + 1}}\)
Given: chain rule
Formula: \(\dfrac{d}{dx}\sqrt{u} = \dfrac{u'}{2\sqrt{u}}\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{2x}{2\sqrt{x^2 + 1}} = \dfrac{x}{\sqrt{x^2 + 1}}\)
Common mistake: (B) forgets \(u' = 2x\). (C) forgets the 2 in the denominator.
Key point: Multiply by the derivative of the inside.

questions.sub_topic: Derivative after simplifying an inverse tangent
questions.question: For \(0 < x < \dfrac{\pi}{4}\), \(\dfrac{d}{dx}\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{\cos x - \sin x}{\cos x + \sin x}\right)\) equals:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(-1\)
Given: divide top and bottom by \(\cos x\): \(\dfrac{1 - \tan x}{1 + \tan x} = \tan\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4} - x\right)\)
Formula: \(\tan^{-1}(\tan\theta) = \theta\) for \(\theta \in \left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)\)
Step 1: The function is \(\dfrac{\pi}{4} - x\)
Step 2: Its derivative is \(-1\)
Common mistake: \(1\) (A) loses the minus sign of \(-x\).
Key point: Simplify inverse trigonometric expressions before differentiating.

questions.sub_topic: Points where y changes twice as fast as x
questions.question: A particle moves along \(y = \dfrac{2}{3}x^3 + 1\). The points at which its \(y\)-coordinate changes twice as fast as its \(x\)-coordinate are:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(\left(1, \dfrac{5}{3}\right)\) and \(\left(-1, \dfrac{1}{3}\right)\)
Given: \(\dfrac{dy}{dt} = 2x^2\dfrac{dx}{dt}\)
Formula: we need \(\dfrac{dy}{dt} = 2\dfrac{dx}{dt}\), so \(2x^2 = 2\)
Step 1: \(x = \pm 1\)
Step 2: \(y(1) = \dfrac{2}{3} + 1 = \dfrac{5}{3}\); \(y(-1) = -\dfrac{2}{3} + 1 = \dfrac{1}{3}\)
Common mistake: (C) gets \(y(-1)\) wrong by forgetting the \(+1\). (A) misses \(x = -1\).
Key point: \(x^2 = 1\) has two roots.

questions.sub_topic: Homogeneous equation y′ = y/x − x/y through (1, 1)
questions.question: The solution of \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{y}{x} - \dfrac{x}{y}\) with \(y(1) = 1\) gives, at \(x = e^{1/4}\) (with \(y > 0\)), \(y\) equal to:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(\dfrac{e^{1/4}}{\sqrt{2}}\)
Given: \(y = vx\): \(v + x\dfrac{dv}{dx} = v - \dfrac{1}{v}\), so \(v\,dv = -\dfrac{dx}{x}\)
Formula: \(\dfrac{v^2}{2} = -\log x + C\), i.e. \(y^2 = x^2(2C - 2\log x)\)
Step 1: \(y(1) = 1\): \(2C = 1\), so \(y^2 = x^2(1 - 2\log x)\)
Step 2: At \(x = e^{1/4}\): \(y^2 = e^{1/2}\left(1 - \dfrac{1}{2}\right) = \dfrac{e^{1/2}}{2}\), so \(y = \dfrac{e^{1/4}}{\sqrt{2}}\)
Common mistake: (C) forgets to take the square root of \(e^{1/2}\).
Key point: Substitute back \(v = \dfrac{y}{x}\) before using the condition.

questions.sub_topic: Line through a point perpendicular to two lines
questions.question: The line through \((1, 2, -4)\) perpendicular to both \(\dfrac{x - 8}{3} = \dfrac{y + 19}{-16} = \dfrac{z - 10}{7}\) and \(\dfrac{x - 15}{3} = \dfrac{y - 29}{8} = \dfrac{z - 5}{-5}\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(\dfrac{x - 1}{2} = \dfrac{y - 2}{3} = \dfrac{z + 4}{6}\)
Given: \(\vec{b}_1 = (3, -16, 7)\), \(\vec{b}_2 = (3, 8, -5)\)
Formula: direction \(= \vec{b}_1 \times \vec{b}_2 = (80 - 56, 21 + 15, 24 + 48) = (24, 36, 72)\), proportional to \((2, 3, 6)\)
Step 1: Through \((1, 2, -4)\): \(\dfrac{x - 1}{2} = \dfrac{y - 2}{3} = \dfrac{z + 4}{6}\)
Common mistake: (B) writes \(z - 4\); the point has \(z = -4\). (A) is parallel to the first line, not perpendicular.
Key point: The cross product of two directions is perpendicular to both.

questions.sub_topic: Vector perpendicular to two vectors with a given dot product
questions.question: \(\vec{a} = \hat{i} + 4\hat{j} + 2\hat{k}\), \(\vec{b} = 3\hat{i} - 2\hat{j} + 7\hat{k}\) and \(\vec{c} = 2\hat{i} - \hat{j} + 4\hat{k}\). The vector \(\vec{d}\) perpendicular to both \(\vec{a}\) and \(\vec{b}\) with \(\vec{c}\cdot\vec{d} = 15\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(\dfrac{1}{3}(160\hat{i} - 5\hat{j} - 70\hat{k})\)
Given: \(\vec{d} = \lambda(\vec{a} \times \vec{b})\)
Formula: \(\vec{a} \times \vec{b} = (28 + 4)\hat{i} - (7 - 6)\hat{j} + (-2 - 12)\hat{k} = 32\hat{i} - \hat{j} - 14\hat{k}\)
Step 1: \(\vec{c}\cdot\vec{d} = \lambda(64 + 1 - 56) = 9\lambda = 15 \Rightarrow \lambda = \dfrac{5}{3}\)
Step 2: \(\vec{d} = \dfrac{5}{3}(32\hat{i} - \hat{j} - 14\hat{k}) = \dfrac{1}{3}(160\hat{i} - 5\hat{j} - 70\hat{k})\)
Common mistake: (A) stops at \(\vec{a} \times \vec{b}\) without scaling. (B) has the wrong sign on \(\hat{j}\).
Key point: The cross product gives the direction; the condition fixes the length.

questions.sub_topic: A sum of 7 and a first die showing 4 — which claims fail
questions.question:
Two dice are thrown. \(E\): the sum is 7; \(F\): the first die shows 4. Consider the following statements:
(A) \(E\) and \(F\) are mutually exclusive.
(B) \(P(E \cap F) = \dfrac{1}{36}\)
(C) \(E\) and \(F\) are independent.
(D) \(P(E \mid F) = \dfrac{1}{6}\)
Which of the statements given above is/are NOT correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A) only
Why: Only (A) is false: the outcome \((4, 3)\) is in both events.
Why not the others: (B) \((4, 3)\) is the only common outcome. (C) \(P(E)P(F) = \dfrac{1}{6} \times \dfrac{1}{6} = \dfrac{1}{36}\). (D) \(\dfrac{1/36}{1/6} = \dfrac{1}{6}\). Options (B), (C) and (D) name a true statement as false.
Key point: Events with a common outcome are not mutually exclusive.

questions.sub_topic: Four values from one 3 × 3 determinant
questions.question:
For \(A = \begin{bmatrix}2&0&1\\1&3&0\\0&1&2\end{bmatrix}\), match List-I with List-II.

List-I
(A) \(|A|\)
(B) The cofactor \(A_{11}\)
(C) \(|\text{adj}\,A|\)
(D) \(|2A|\)

List-II
(I) \(169\)
(II) \(13\)
(III) \(6\)
(IV) \(104\)
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A)-(II), (B)-(III), (C)-(I), (D)-(IV)
Step 1: \(|A| = 2(6 - 0) - 0 + 1(1 - 0) = 13\) (II)
Step 2: \(A_{11} = 3 \times 2 - 0 \times 1 = 6\) (III)
Step 3: \(|\text{adj}\,A| = 13^2 = 169\) (I)
Step 4: \(|2A| = 2^3 \times 13 = 104\) (IV)
Common mistake: Taking \(|2A| = 26\), forgetting that each of the three rows is doubled.
Key point: For order 3, \(|\text{adj}\,A| = |A|^2\) and \(|2A| = 8|A|\).

questions.sub_topic: Order of y″ + sin(y′) = 0
questions.question: The order of the differential equation \(\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} + \sin\left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right) = 0\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(2\)
Given: the highest derivative is \(\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}\)
Formula: order = order of the highest derivative
Step 1: 2
Common mistake: (D) confuses order with degree; the degree is not defined because of \(\sin y'\), but the order is.
Key point: Order is always defined; degree needs a polynomial in the derivatives.

questions.sub_topic: Derivative of (log x)^(cos x) at x = e
questions.question: If \(y = (\log x)^{\cos x}\) (\(x > 1\)), then \(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\) at \(x = e\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(\dfrac{\cos e}{e}\)
Given: \(\log y = \cos x \cdot \log(\log x)\)
Formula: \(\dfrac{y'}{y} = -\sin x\log(\log x) + \dfrac{\cos x}{x\log x}\)
Step 1: At \(x = e\): \(\log e = 1\), \(\log(\log e) = 0\), \(y = 1^{\cos e} = 1\)
Step 2: \(y' = 1 \times \left(0 + \dfrac{\cos e}{e}\right) = \dfrac{\cos e}{e}\)
Common mistake: \(-\sin e\) (B) keeps only the first term without noticing \(\log(\log e) = 0\).
Key point: Take logs before differentiating a variable power.

questions.sub_topic: Point on y² = 4x nearest to (2, 1)
questions.question: The point on the parabola \(y^2 = 4x\) nearest to \((2, 1)\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \((1, 2)\)
Given: point \(\left(\dfrac{y^2}{4}, y\right)\)
Formula: \(D = \left(\dfrac{y^2}{4} - 2\right)^2 + (y - 1)^2\)
Step 1: \(D'(y) = 2\left(\dfrac{y^2}{4} - 2\right)\dfrac{y}{2} + 2(y - 1) = \dfrac{y^3}{4} - 2 = 0 \Rightarrow y = 2\)
Step 2: \(D'' = \dfrac{3y^2}{4} > 0\), a minimum; the point is \((1, 2)\)
Common mistake: \((1, -2)\) (B) takes the wrong sign of \(y\). (D) has the same \(x\) as the given point, which is not the nearest.
Key point: Minimise the squared distance to avoid square roots.

questions.sub_topic: Definite integral of 1/(1 + √tan x) on [π/6, π/3]
questions.question: \(\displaystyle\int_{\pi/6}^{\pi/3}\dfrac{dx}{1 + \sqrt{\tan x}}\) equals:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(\dfrac{\pi}{12}\)
Given: \(\int_a^b f(x)\,dx = \int_a^b f(a + b - x)\,dx\), with \(a + b = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\)
Formula: \(\tan\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2} - x\right) = \cot x\), so \(I = \int\dfrac{\sqrt{\tan x}}{\sqrt{\tan x} + 1}\,dx\)
Step 1: Adding the two forms: \(2I = \int_{\pi/6}^{\pi/3}1\,dx = \dfrac{\pi}{6}\)
Step 2: \(I = \dfrac{\pi}{12}\)
Common mistake: \(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\) (A) forgets to halve.
Key point: Use \(a + b - x\) for limits that are not 0 and \(a\).

questions.sub_topic: The relation b = a + 1 on {1, …, 6}
questions.question: On \(A = \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\}\), let \(R = \{(a, b) : b = a + 1\}\). Then \(R\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) none of the three
Why: \((1, 1) \notin R\), so not reflexive. \((1, 2) \in R\) but \((2, 1) \notin R\), so not symmetric. \((1, 2), (2, 3) \in R\) but \((1, 3) \notin R\), so not transitive.
Why not the others: Each of (A), (B), (C) claims one of the properties that fails.
Key point: One counter-example is enough to rule out a property.

questions.sub_topic: Two perpendicular vectors — which hold
questions.question:
For \(\vec{a} = \hat{i} + \hat{j} + \hat{k}\) and \(\vec{b} = \hat{i} - 2\hat{j} + \hat{k}\), consider the following statements:
(A) \(\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} = 0\)
(B) \(|\vec{a} \times \vec{b}| = |\vec{a}||\vec{b}|\)
(C) \(\vec{a} \times \vec{b} = 3\hat{i} - 3\hat{k}\)
(D) The projection of \(\vec{a}\) on \(\vec{b}\) is 1.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: \(1 - 2 + 1 = 0\), so (A) holds and \(\sin\theta = 1\) gives (B). \(\vec{a} \times \vec{b} = (1 + 2)\hat{i} - (1 - 1)\hat{j} + (-2 - 1)\hat{k}\), so (C) holds.
Why not the others: (D) is false: the projection is \(\dfrac{\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b}}{|\vec{b}|} = 0\). Options (C) and (D) include (D); option (B) omits statement (B).
Key point: Perpendicular vectors have zero projection on each other.

questions.sub_topic: Linear equation x y′ + y = x log x
questions.question: The general solution of \(x\dfrac{dy}{dx} + y = x\log x\) (\(x > 0\)) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(y = \dfrac{x}{2}\log x - \dfrac{x}{4} + \dfrac{C}{x}\)
Given: the left side is \(\dfrac{d}{dx}(xy)\)
Formula: \(xy = \int x\log x\,dx = \dfrac{x^2}{2}\log x - \dfrac{x^2}{4} + C\) (by parts)
Step 1: Divide by \(x\): \(y = \dfrac{x}{2}\log x - \dfrac{x}{4} + \dfrac{C}{x}\)
Common mistake: (C) gets the sign of \(\int\dfrac{x}{2}\,dx\) wrong in the parts step. (D) forgets to divide by \(x\).
Key point: Spot an exact derivative on the left.

questions.sub_topic: Integral of 1/√x
questions.question: \(\displaystyle\int\dfrac{dx}{\sqrt{x}}\) equals:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(2\sqrt{x} + C\)
Given: \(x^{-1/2}\)
Formula: \(\int x^n\,dx = \dfrac{x^{n+1}}{n + 1}\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{x^{1/2}}{1/2} = 2\sqrt{x}\)
Common mistake: (A) multiplies by \(\dfrac{1}{2}\) instead of dividing. (B) differentiates.
Key point: Dividing by \(\dfrac{1}{2}\) doubles.

questions.sub_topic: Four standard integrals — which claims fail
questions.question:
Consider the following statements (constants omitted):
(A) \(\displaystyle\int e^x(\sin x + \cos x)\,dx = e^x\cos x\)
(B) \(\displaystyle\int\dfrac{dx}{x\log x} = \log|\log x|\)
(C) \(\displaystyle\int\tan x\,dx = \log|\sec x|\)
(D) \(\displaystyle\int\dfrac{dx}{1 + x^2} = \tan^{-1}x\)
Which of the statements given above is/are NOT correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A) only
Why: Only (A) is false: with \(f = \sin x\), \(f' = \cos x\), so \(\int e^x(f + f')\,dx = e^x\sin x\).
Why not the others: (B) \(t = \log x\). (C) \(\log|\sec x| = -\log|\cos x|\). (D) a standard result. Options (B), (C) and (D) name a true statement as false.
Key point: In \(e^x(f + f')\), the answer uses \(f\), not \(f'\).

questions.topic: Unit III: Applications of the Integrals
questions.sub_topic: Areas of four regions
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I
(A) Area inside \(x^2 + y^2 = 16\) in the first quadrant
(B) Area under \(y = e^x\) from \(x = 0\) to \(x = \log 3\)
(C) Area between \(y = x\) and \(y = x^3\) in the first quadrant
(D) Area enclosed by \(\dfrac{x^2}{4} + y^2 = 1\)

List-II
(I) \(2\pi\)
(II) \(\dfrac{1}{4}\)
(III) \(4\pi\)
(IV) \(2\)
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A)-(III), (B)-(IV), (C)-(II), (D)-(I)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{1}{4}\pi(4)^2 = 4\pi\) (III)
Step 2: \(\left[e^x\right]_0^{\log 3} = 3 - 1 = 2\) (IV)
Step 3: \(\int_0^1(x - x^3)\,dx = \dfrac{1}{2} - \dfrac{1}{4} = \dfrac{1}{4}\) (II)
Step 4: \(\pi ab = \pi(2)(1) = 2\pi\) (I)
Common mistake: Writing \(16\pi\) for (A), the whole circle instead of one quadrant.
Key point: An ellipse has area \(\pi ab\).

questions.sub_topic: No black ball in four draws with replacement
questions.question: A bag has 5 white, 7 red and 8 black balls. Four balls are drawn one by one with replacement. The probability that none is black is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(\dfrac{81}{625}\)
Given: \(P(\text{not black}) = \dfrac{12}{20} = \dfrac{3}{5}\) on each draw
Formula: independent draws multiply
Step 1: \(\left(\dfrac{3}{5}\right)^4 = \dfrac{81}{625}\)
Common mistake: \(\dfrac{16}{625}\) (A) is "all black". \(\dfrac{544}{625}\) (D) is "at least one black".
Key point: With replacement the draws are independent.

questions.sub_topic: Where x − 2 sin x increases on [0, 2π]
questions.question: On \([0, 2\pi]\), the function \(f(x) = x - 2\sin x\) is strictly increasing on:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}, \dfrac{5\pi}{3}\right)\)
Given: \(f'(x) = 1 - 2\cos x\)
Formula: \(f' > 0 \iff \cos x < \dfrac{1}{2}\)
Step 1: On \([0, 2\pi]\), \(\cos x < \dfrac{1}{2}\) for \(\dfrac{\pi}{3} < x < \dfrac{5\pi}{3}\)
Common mistake: (A) and (C) are where \(f\) decreases. (D) stops at \(\pi\).
Key point: Solve the trigonometric inequality over the whole interval.

questions.sub_topic: Bayes' theorem: how a late doctor travelled
questions.question: A doctor comes by train, bus, scooter or other means with probabilities \(\dfrac{3}{10}\), \(\dfrac{1}{5}\), \(\dfrac{1}{10}\) and \(\dfrac{2}{5}\). The probabilities of being late are \(\dfrac{1}{4}\), \(\dfrac{1}{3}\) and \(\dfrac{1}{12}\) for train, bus and scooter, and 0 otherwise. The doctor is late. The probability that the doctor came by train is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(\dfrac{1}{2}\)
Given: \(P(L) = \dfrac{3}{10} \times \dfrac{1}{4} + \dfrac{1}{5} \times \dfrac{1}{3} + \dfrac{1}{10} \times \dfrac{1}{12} + 0\)
Formula: \(P(T \mid L) = \dfrac{P(T)P(L \mid T)}{P(L)}\)
Step 1: \(P(L) = \dfrac{9}{120} + \dfrac{8}{120} + \dfrac{1}{120} = \dfrac{18}{120}\)
Step 2: \(P(T \mid L) = \dfrac{9/120}{18/120} = \dfrac{1}{2}\)
Common mistake: \(\dfrac{4}{9}\) (B) is the bus. \(\dfrac{1}{18}\) (D) is the scooter.
Key point: A cause with zero likelihood drops out of the sum.

questions.sub_topic: Bijections of {1, 2, 3} that move 1
questions.question: The number of one-one functions \(f: \{1, 2, 3\} \to \{1, 2, 3\}\) with \(f(1) \ne 1\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(4\)
Given: there are \(3! = 6\) one-one functions in all
Formula: subtract those with \(f(1) = 1\)
Step 1: With \(f(1) = 1\), \(f(2), f(3)\) can be arranged in \(2! = 2\) ways
Step 2: \(6 - 2 = 4\)
Common mistake: \(6\) (A) ignores the condition. \(2\) (C) counts the excluded ones.
Key point: Count the complement when it is easier.

questions.sub_topic: Transpose of an upper triangular 2 × 2 matrix
questions.question: For \(A = \begin{bmatrix}2&-1\\0&3\end{bmatrix}\), \(A^T\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(\begin{bmatrix}2&0\\-1&3\end{bmatrix}\)
Given: rows become columns
Formula: \((A^T)_{ij} = a_{ji}\)
Step 1: First row \((2, -1)\) becomes the first column
Common mistake: (C) is \(-A\). (D) also swaps the diagonal entries.
Key point: The diagonal stays put under a transpose.

questions.sub_topic: Symmetric 2 × 2 matrices with entries 0 or 1
questions.question: The number of symmetric matrices of order \(2 \times 2\) whose entries are 0 or 1 is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(8\)
Given: symmetric means \(a_{12} = a_{21}\)
Formula: free entries \(a_{11}, a_{22}, a_{12}\), each with 2 choices
Step 1: \(2^3 = 8\)
Common mistake: \(16\) (A) counts all \(2 \times 2\) matrices.
Key point: Count only the entries you are free to choose.

questions.sub_topic: Simplifying cos⁻¹(cos 10)
questions.question: \(\cos^{-1}(\cos 10)\) equals (angle in radians):
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(4\pi - 10\)
Given: \(\cos^{-1}(\cos\theta) = \theta\) only for \(\theta \in [0, \pi]\)
Formula: \(\cos\) has period \(2\pi\) and \(\cos(-\theta) = \cos\theta\)
Step 1: \(\cos 10 = \cos(10 - 4\pi) = \cos(4\pi - 10)\)
Step 2: \(4\pi - 10 \approx 2.57\), which lies in \([0, \pi]\)
Common mistake: \(10 - 2\pi \approx 3.72\) (B) is greater than \(\pi\). (A) is negative.
Key point: Bring the angle into \([0, \pi]\) using \(2\pi k \pm \theta\).

questions.sub_topic: Image of a point in a line
questions.question: The image of the point \((1, 6, 3)\) in the line \(\dfrac{x}{1} = \dfrac{y - 1}{2} = \dfrac{z - 2}{3}\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \((1, 0, 7)\)
Given: a general point of the line is \((\lambda, 1 + 2\lambda, 2 + 3\lambda)\)
Formula: the foot \(F\) makes \(\vec{PF} \perp (1, 2, 3)\)
Step 1: \((\lambda - 1) + 2(2\lambda - 5) + 3(3\lambda - 1) = 14\lambda - 14 = 0 \Rightarrow \lambda = 1\), \(F = (1, 3, 5)\)
Step 2: Image \(= 2F - P = (2 - 1, 6 - 6, 10 - 3) = (1, 0, 7)\)
Common mistake: (A) is the foot of the perpendicular, not the image.
Key point: The foot is the midpoint of the point and its image.

questions.sub_topic: Is 2x plus the modulus of x a bijection?
questions.question: The function \(f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}\), \(f(x) = 2x + |x|\), is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) both one-one and onto
Why: \(f(x) = 3x\) for \(x \ge 0\) and \(f(x) = x\) for \(x < 0\). Both pieces are strictly increasing and they join at 0, so \(f\) is one-one. The first piece covers \([0, \infty)\) and the second \((-\infty, 0)\), so \(f\) is onto.
Why not the others: (B), (D) miss that the negative values come from \(x < 0\). (C), (D) miss that \(f\) is strictly increasing.
Key point: Split a modulus function into pieces before testing.

questions.question: The value of \(\tan^{-1}(-1) + \cos^{-1}\left(-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\)
Given: \(\tan^{-1}(-1) = -\dfrac{\pi}{4}\)
Formula: \(\cos^{-1}(-x) = \pi - \cos^{-1}x\), so \(\cos^{-1}\left(-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right) = \dfrac{3\pi}{4}\)
Step 1: \(-\dfrac{\pi}{4} + \dfrac{3\pi}{4} = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\)
Common mistake: \(-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\) (D) takes \(\cos^{-1}\left(-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right) = -\dfrac{\pi}{4}\), outside \([0, \pi]\).
Key point: \(\cos^{-1}\) of a negative number lies in \(\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \pi\right]\).

questions.sub_topic: Values from a five-cornered region for 5x + 2y
questions.question:
For \(Z = 5x + 2y\) subject to \(x + y \ge 2\), \(x \le 4\), \(y \le 3\), \(x, y \ge 0\), match List-I with List-II.

List-I
(A) The minimum value of \(Z\)
(B) The point where the minimum occurs
(C) The maximum value of \(Z\)
(D) The number of corner points of the feasible region

List-II
(I) \(4\)
(II) \(26\)
(III) \(5\)
(IV) \((0, 2)\)
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A)-(I), (B)-(IV), (C)-(II), (D)-(III)
Step 1: Corners \((2, 0)\), \((4, 0)\), \((4, 3)\), \((0, 3)\), \((0, 2)\): five in all (III)
Step 2: \(Z = 10, 20, 26, 6, 4\)
Step 3: Minimum 4 (I) at \((0, 2)\) (IV)
Step 4: Maximum 26 at \((4, 3)\) (II)
Common mistake: Taking the origin as the minimum; it is cut off by \(x + y \ge 2\).
Key point: A "\(\ge\)" constraint removes the corner at the origin.

questions.sub_topic: Area of a triangle with negative coordinates
questions.question: The area of the triangle with vertices \((-2, -3)\), \((3, 2)\) and \((-1, -8)\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(15\)
Given: \(\Delta = \dfrac{1}{2}\left|x_1(y_2 - y_3) + x_2(y_3 - y_1) + x_3(y_1 - y_2)\right|\)
Formula: substitute the vertices
Step 1: \(-2(2 + 8) + 3(-8 + 3) + (-1)(-3 - 2) = -20 - 15 + 5 = -30\)
Step 2: Area \(= \dfrac{1}{2}|-30| = 15\)
Common mistake: \(30\) (A) forgets the \(\dfrac{1}{2}\).
Key point: Take the modulus; area is never negative.

questions.sub_topic: An unbounded region where Z has no maximum — which claims fail
questions.question:
For \(Z = -x + 2y\) subject to \(x \ge 3\), \(x + y \ge 5\), \(x + 2y \ge 6\), \(y \ge 0\), consider the following statements:
(A) The feasible region is unbounded.
(B) The maximum value of \(Z\) is 1, at \((3, 2)\).
(C) \((4, 1)\) is a corner point.
(D) \(Z = -6\) at \((6, 0)\).
Which of the statements given above is/are NOT correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (B) only
Why: Corners \((6, 0)\), \((4, 1)\), \((3, 2)\) give \(Z = -6, -2, 1\). Only (B) is false: the half-plane \(-x + 2y > 1\) contains points of the region (e.g. \((3, 10)\)), so \(Z\) has no maximum.
Why not the others: (A) nothing bounds \(x\) or \(y\) from above. (C) \(x + y = 5\) meets \(x + 2y = 6\) at \((4, 1)\). (D) \(-6 + 0 = -6\). Options (A), (C) and (D) name a true statement as false.
Key point: On an unbounded region, test the open half-plane before claiming an optimum.

questions.sub_topic: Marginal revenue from a linear demand at x = 10
questions.question: The demand function is \(p = 100 - 2x\). The marginal revenue when \(x = 10\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(60\)
Given: \(R = px = 100x - 2x^2\)
Formula: \(MR = \dfrac{dR}{dx} = 100 - 4x\)
Step 1: \(100 - 40 = 60\)
Common mistake: \(80\) (A) is the price at \(x = 10\). \(800\) (D) is the revenue.
Key point: Marginal revenue falls twice as fast as price for a linear demand.

questions.sub_topic: Least cost of a diet with two foods and two nutrients
questions.question: Food F₁ costs ₹4 per unit and gives 3 units of vitamin A and 4 units of minerals. Food F₂ costs ₹6 per unit and gives 6 units of vitamin A and 3 units of minerals. At least 80 units of vitamin A and 100 units of minerals are needed. The least cost is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) ₹104
Given: \(3x + 6y \ge 80\), \(4x + 3y \ge 100\), \(x, y \ge 0\); \(Z = 4x + 6y\)
Formula: corners \(\left(\dfrac{80}{3}, 0\right)\), \(\left(24, \dfrac{4}{3}\right)\), \(\left(0, \dfrac{100}{3}\right)\)
Step 1: \(Z = 106.67, 104, 200\)
Step 2: \(4x + 6y < 104\) has no point in the region, so the least cost is ₹104
Common mistake: ₹106.67 (A) skips the corner where the two lines meet.
Key point: Solve \(3x + 6y = 80\) and \(4x + 3y = 100\): \(5x = 120\), \(x = 24\).

questions.sub_topic: Determinant, adjoint, inverse and a multiple of one matrix
questions.question:
For \(A = \begin{bmatrix}4&2\\3&1\end{bmatrix}\), match List-I with List-II.

List-I
(A) \(|A|\)
(B) \(\text{adj}\,A\)
(C) \(A^{-1}\)
(D) \(|3A|\)

List-II
(I) \(\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{2}&1\\\frac{3}{2}&-2\end{bmatrix}\)
(II) \(-18\)
(III) \(\begin{bmatrix}1&-2\\-3&4\end{bmatrix}\)
(IV) \(-2\)
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A)-(IV), (B)-(III), (C)-(I), (D)-(II)
Step 1: \(|A| = 4 - 6 = -2\) (IV)
Step 2: Swap the diagonal, change the other signs: \(\begin{bmatrix}1&-2\\-3&4\end{bmatrix}\) (III)
Step 3: \(A^{-1} = \dfrac{1}{-2}\text{adj}\,A\) (I)
Step 4: \(|3A| = 3^2(-2) = -18\) (II)
Common mistake: Taking \(|3A| = -6\), using \(3|A|\) instead of \(3^2|A|\).
Key point: For order 2, \(|kA| = k^2|A|\).

questions.topic: Unit I: Numbers, Quantification and Numerical Applications
questions.sub_topic: Value of 47 mod 6
questions.question: The value of \(47 \bmod 6\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(5\)
Given: \(47 = 7 \times 6 + 5\)
Formula: the remainder lies in \(\{0, 1, \ldots, 5\}\)
Step 1: \(47 \bmod 6 = 5\)
Common mistake: \(7\) (C) is the quotient.
Key point: The remainder is less than the divisor.

questions.sub_topic: Definite integral of eˣ/(1 + eˣ) on [0, log 2]
questions.question: \(\displaystyle\int_0^{\log 2}\dfrac{e^x}{1 + e^x}\,dx\) equals:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(\log\dfrac{3}{2}\)
Given: the numerator is the derivative of \(1 + e^x\)
Formula: \(\left[\log(1 + e^x)\right]_0^{\log 2}\)
Step 1: \(\log 3 - \log 2 = \log\dfrac{3}{2}\)
Common mistake: \(\log 3\) (C) forgets the lower limit, where \(1 + e^0 = 2\).
Key point: At \(x = 0\) the value is \(\log 2\), not 0.

questions.topic: Unit I: Numbers, Quantification and Numerical Applications
questions.sub_topic: One race with two margins — which hold
questions.question:
In a 1 km race, A beats B by 100 m and B beats C by 100 m. Consider the following statements:
(A) A beats C by 190 m.
(B) The speeds of A and B are in the ratio \(10 : 9\).
(C) If A gives C a start of 190 m, the race ends in a dead heat.
(D) The speeds of B and C are in the ratio \(10 : 8\).
Which of the statements given above are correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: While A runs 1000 m, B runs 900 m and C runs \(0.9 \times 900 = 810\) m, so A beats C by 190 m. (B) \(1000 : 900\). (C) follows from (A).
Why not the others: (D) is false: B runs 1000 while C runs 900, so \(10 : 9\). Options (C) and (D) include (D); (B) leaves out (C).
Key point: Margins combine by multiplying ratios, not by adding.

questions.sub_topic: EMIs, sinking funds, CAGR and depreciation — which hold
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) In an EMI on a reducing balance, the interest part of each instalment falls over time.
(B) A sinking fund builds up money to meet a future liability.
(C) CAGR \(= \left(\dfrac{\text{final value}}{\text{initial value}}\right)^{1/n} - 1\).
(D) Under the straight-line method, the book value falls by the same percentage each year.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: (A) interest is charged on a shrinking balance. (B) that is the purpose of a sinking fund. (C) the definition of CAGR.
Why not the others: (D) is false: the straight-line method removes the same amount each year, so the percentage rises as the book value falls. Options (C) and (D) include (D); (A) leaves out (C).
Key point: Straight-line means a constant amount, not a constant rate.

questions.topic: Unit I: Numbers, Quantification and Numerical Applications
questions.sub_topic: Ratio for mixing two gold–copper alloys
questions.question: Two alloys contain gold and copper in the ratios \(2 : 3\) and \(3 : 7\). In what ratio must they be mixed to get an alloy with gold and copper in the ratio \(5 : 11\)?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(1 : 7\)
Given: gold fractions \(\dfrac{2}{5} = 0.4\), \(\dfrac{3}{10} = 0.3\), target \(\dfrac{5}{16} = 0.3125\)
Formula: first : second \(= (0.3125 - 0.3) : (0.4 - 0.3125)\)
Step 1: \(0.0125 : 0.0875 = 1 : 7\)
Step 2: Check: \(\dfrac{0.4 + 7(0.3)}{8} = \dfrac{2.5}{8} = 0.3125\) ✓
Common mistake: \(7 : 1\) (A) reverses the ratio; the target is close to the second alloy, so more of it is needed.
Key point: Use the fraction of gold, not the gold : copper ratio, in the alligation.

questions.sub_topic: Integral of eˣ(x + 1)
questions.question: \(\displaystyle\int e^x(x + 1)\,dx\) equals:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(xe^x + C\)
Given: \(\int e^x(f + f')\,dx = e^xf + C\)
Formula: \(f = x\), \(f' = 1\)
Step 1: \(xe^x + C\)
Common mistake: (A) differentiates to \((x + 2)e^x\), not \((x + 1)e^x\).
Key point: Check by differentiating: \((xe^x)' = e^x + xe^x\) ✓.

questions.topic: Unit I: Numbers, Quantification and Numerical Applications
questions.sub_topic: A system of two linear inequalities
questions.question: The solution of \(2x - 3 > 5\) and \(3x + 4 \le 25\) together is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \((4, 7]\)
Given: \(2x > 8 \Rightarrow x > 4\); \(3x \le 21 \Rightarrow x \le 7\)
Formula: take the common part
Step 1: \(4 < x \le 7\), i.e. \((4, 7]\)
Common mistake: (B) swaps which end is included.
Key point: Strict inequality gives an open end.

questions.sub_topic: Normal probability between one and two SDs above the mean
questions.question: \(X\) is normal with mean 50 and SD 4. Given \(P(0 < Z < 1) = 0.3413\) and \(P(0 < Z < 2) = 0.4772\), \(P(54 < X < 58)\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(0.1359\)
Given: \(z = \dfrac{54 - 50}{4} = 1\) and \(\dfrac{58 - 50}{4} = 2\)
Formula: \(P(1 < Z < 2) = P(0 < Z < 2) - P(0 < Z < 1)\)
Step 1: \(0.4772 - 0.3413 = 0.1359\)
Common mistake: \(0.8185\) (A) adds the areas, as for an interval on both sides of the mean.
Key point: For an interval on one side of the mean, subtract.

questions.sub_topic: Differential equation of y = Aeˣ + Be^(2x)
questions.question: The differential equation of the family \(y = Ae^x + Be^{2x}\) (\(A\), \(B\) arbitrary) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(y'' - 3y' + 2y = 0\)
Given: \(y' = Ae^x + 2Be^{2x}\), \(y'' = Ae^x + 4Be^{2x}\)
Formula: eliminate \(A\) and \(B\)
Step 1: \(y'' - 3y' + 2y = A(1 - 3 + 2)e^x + B(4 - 6 + 2)e^{2x} = 0\)
Common mistake: (B) gives the equation for \(e^{-x}\) and \(e^{-2x}\).
Key point: Roots 1 and 2 give \(m^2 - 3m + 2 = 0\).

questions.topic: Unit I: Numbers, Quantification and Numerical Applications
questions.sub_topic: Boat speeds from two journeys of equal time
questions.question: A boat goes 24 km upstream and 36 km downstream in 6 hours, and 36 km upstream and 24 km downstream in 6.5 hours. The speed of the stream is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(2\) km/h
Given: let \(u = \dfrac{1}{\text{upstream speed}}\), \(d = \dfrac{1}{\text{downstream speed}}\)
Formula: \(24u + 36d = 6\) and \(36u + 24d = 6.5\)
Step 1: Adding: \(60(u + d) = 12.5\); subtracting: \(12(u - d) = 0.5\); so \(u = \dfrac{1}{8}\), \(d = \dfrac{1}{12}\)
Step 2: Upstream 8, downstream 12 km/h; stream \(= \dfrac{12 - 8}{2} = 2\) km/h
Common mistake: \(10\) km/h (A) is the speed in still water. \(4\) km/h (B) forgets to halve the difference.
Key point: Use reciprocals of the speeds as the unknowns.

questions.sub_topic: Third centred four-yearly moving average
questions.question: For the values 30, 34, 38, 36, 40, 44, 46 over seven years, the third centred four-yearly moving average is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(40.5\)
Given: four-yearly totals: 138, 148, 158, 166
Formula: centred values \(= \dfrac{\text{two neighbouring totals}}{8}\)
Step 1: First \(\dfrac{286}{8} = 35.75\); second \(\dfrac{306}{8} = 38.25\)
Step 2: Third \(\dfrac{158 + 166}{8} = \dfrac{324}{8} = 40.5\)
Common mistake: \(38.25\) (B) is the second centred value. \(41.5\) (A) is the uncentred average \(\dfrac{166}{4}\).
Key point: Divide the sum of two four-year totals by 8.

questions.sub_topic: Amount of a three-year annuity
questions.question: ₹3,000 is deposited at the end of each year for 3 years at 10% compounded annually. The amount at the end of 3 years is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) ₹9,930
Given: deposits earn 2, 1 and 0 years of interest
Formula: \(A = 3000(1.1^2 + 1.1 + 1)\)
Step 1: \(3000(1.21 + 1.1 + 1) = 3000 \times 3.31\)
Step 2: \(= ₹9{,}930\)
Common mistake: ₹10,923 (D) gives every deposit an extra year (deposits at the start). ₹9,000 (A) ignores interest.
Key point: The last deposit earns no interest.

questions.sub_topic: Local maximum value of 2x³ − 3x² − 12x + 1
questions.question: The local maximum value of \(f(x) = 2x^3 - 3x^2 - 12x + 1\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(8\)
Given: \(f'(x) = 6x^2 - 6x - 12 = 6(x - 2)(x + 1)\)
Formula: \(f''(x) = 12x - 6\); \(f''(-1) < 0\), a maximum
Step 1: \(f(-1) = -2 - 3 + 12 + 1 = 8\)
Common mistake: \(-19\) (B) is the local minimum value, at \(x = 2\). \(-1\) (C) is the point.
Key point: Give the value of \(f\), not the point.

questions.sub_topic: Outstanding balance after two EMIs
questions.question: A loan of ₹1,00,000 at 1% interest per month is repaid by 12 monthly EMIs of ₹8,884.88. The outstanding balance just after the second EMI is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) ₹84,151.39
Given: balance \(B_0 = 1{,}00{,}000\), EMI ₹8,884.88
Formula: \(B_{k} = B_{k-1}(1.01) - \text{EMI}\)
Step 1: \(B_1 = 1{,}01{,}000 - 8{,}884.88 = 92{,}115.12\)
Step 2: \(B_2 = 92{,}115.12 + 921.15 - 8{,}884.88 = ₹84{,}151.39\)
Common mistake: ₹82,230.24 (B) subtracts two EMIs and ignores interest. ₹92,115.12 (C) is the balance after one EMI.
Key point: Add the month's interest before taking off each EMI.

questions.sub_topic: Binomial probability from the mean and variance
questions.question: A binomial variable \(X\) has mean 6 and variance 2. Then \(P(X = 9)\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(\left(\dfrac{2}{3}\right)^9\)
Given: \(np = 6\), \(npq = 2\)
Formula: \(q = \dfrac{2}{6} = \dfrac{1}{3}\), \(p = \dfrac{2}{3}\), \(n = \dfrac{6}{2/3} = 9\)
Step 1: \(P(X = 9) = \binom{9}{9}p^9 = \left(\dfrac{2}{3}\right)^9\)
Common mistake: (A) uses \(q\) for \(p\). (D) is \(P(X = 8)\).
Key point: Divide the variance by the mean to get \(q\).

questions.sub_topic: Inverse from A² − 4A + 3I = O
questions.question: For \(A = \begin{bmatrix}2&-1\\-1&2\end{bmatrix}\), \(A^2 - 4A + 3I = O\). Hence \(A^{-1}\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(\dfrac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{bmatrix}\)
Given: \(A^2 - 4A = -3I\)
Formula: multiply by \(A^{-1}\): \(A - 4I = -3A^{-1}\), so \(A^{-1} = \dfrac{1}{3}(4I - A)\)
Step 1: \(4I - A = \begin{bmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{bmatrix}\)
Step 2: \(A^{-1} = \dfrac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{bmatrix}\); check \(|A| = 3\) ✓
Common mistake: (B) forgets the \(\dfrac{1}{3}\). (C) is \(\dfrac{1}{3}A\).
Key point: Multiply the identity by \(A^{-1}\) and solve.

questions.sub_topic: t-statistic from five observations with μ₀ = 13
questions.question: A sample gives 12, 14, 15, 17, 22. To test \(H_0: \mu = 13\), the \(t\)-statistic is about:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(1.76\)
Given: \(\bar{x} = \dfrac{80}{5} = 16\); deviations \(-4, -2, -1, 1, 6\)
Formula: \(s^2 = \dfrac{\sum(x - \bar{x})^2}{n - 1}\), \(t = \dfrac{\bar{x} - \mu_0}{s/\sqrt{n}}\)
Step 1: \(\sum(x - \bar{x})^2 = 16 + 4 + 1 + 1 + 36 = 58\), \(s^2 = 14.5\)
Step 2: SE \(= \sqrt{\dfrac{14.5}{5}} = \sqrt{2.9} \approx 1.703\); \(t = \dfrac{3}{1.703} \approx 1.76\)
Common mistake: \(1.97\) (A) divides by \(n = 5\) instead of 4. \(0.79\) (C) divides by \(s\) rather than the SE.
Key point: SE \(= \dfrac{s}{\sqrt{n}}\), with \(s\) using \(n - 1\).

questions.sub_topic: Poisson probability of at most two with mean 1
questions.question: For a Poisson distribution with mean 1, \(P(X \le 2)\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(\dfrac{5}{2e}\)
Given: \(P(X = r) = \dfrac{e^{-1}}{r!}\)
Formula: \(P(X \le 2) = e^{-1}\left(1 + 1 + \dfrac{1}{2}\right)\)
Step 1: \(= \dfrac{5}{2e}\)
Common mistake: \(\dfrac{2}{e}\) (B) stops at \(X \le 1\). \(\dfrac{3}{e}\) (D) forgets the \(2!\).
Key point: Include \(r = 0\).

questions.sub_topic: Total surplus at market equilibrium with quadratic curves
questions.question: The demand function is \(p = 20 - x^2\) and the supply function is \(p = 2 + x^2\). The total of consumer and producer surplus at equilibrium is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(36\)
Given: \(20 - x^2 = 2 + x^2 \Rightarrow x_0 = 3\), \(p_0 = 11\)
Formula: \(CS = \int_0^3(20 - x^2)\,dx - 33\), \(PS = 33 - \int_0^3(2 + x^2)\,dx\)
Step 1: \(CS = 60 - 9 - 33 = 18\)
Step 2: \(PS = 33 - (6 + 9) = 18\); total \(= 36\)
Common mistake: \(18\) (A) gives only one of the two surpluses. \(33\) (B) is \(p_0x_0\).
Key point: Total surplus is the area between the demand and supply curves.

questions.sub_topic: Sample size for a target standard error
questions.question: A population has standard deviation 12. The smallest sample size for which the standard error of the mean is at most 1.5 is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(64\)
Given: SE \(= \dfrac{12}{\sqrt{n}} \le 1.5\)
Formula: \(\sqrt{n} \ge \dfrac{12}{1.5} = 8\)
Step 1: \(n \ge 64\)
Common mistake: \(8\) (B) stops at \(\sqrt{n}\).
Key point: Square at the end.

questions.sub_topic: A one-sample t-test with n = 16 from start to decision
questions.question:
A sample of 16 has mean 104 and standard deviation 8 (divisor \(n - 1\)). \(H_0: \mu = 101\) is tested at the 5% level (two-tailed), with \(t_{0.025, 15} = 2.131\). Match List-I with List-II.

List-I
(A) Degrees of freedom
(B) Standard error of the mean
(C) The \(t\)-statistic
(D) The decision

List-II
(I) \(2\)
(II) Do not reject \(H_0\)
(III) \(15\)
(IV) \(1.5\)
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A)-(III), (B)-(I), (C)-(IV), (D)-(II)
Step 1: df \(= 16 - 1 = 15\) (III)
Step 2: SE \(= \dfrac{8}{\sqrt{16}} = 2\) (I)
Step 3: \(t = \dfrac{104 - 101}{2} = 1.5\) (IV)
Step 4: \(1.5 < 2.131\), so do not reject \(H_0\) (II)
Common mistake: Rejecting \(H_0\) because the sample mean is above 101; the difference must exceed the critical value in SE units.
Key point: Compare \(|t|\) with the table value.

questions.sub_topic: Values from binomial, uniform and normal distributions
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I
(A) Variance of a binomial distribution with \(n = 12\), \(p = \dfrac{1}{3}\)
(B) Mean score on a fair die
(C) Standard normal variate for \(X = 82\) when \(\mu = 70\), \(\sigma = 8\)
(D) \(P(Z > 0)\) for the standard normal variable

List-II
(I) \(3.5\)
(II) \(\dfrac{8}{3}\)
(III) \(0.5\)
(IV) \(1.5\)
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A)-(II), (B)-(I), (C)-(IV), (D)-(III)
Step 1: \(npq = 12 \times \dfrac{1}{3} \times \dfrac{2}{3} = \dfrac{8}{3}\) (II)
Step 2: \(\dfrac{1 + 2 + \cdots + 6}{6} = 3.5\) (I)
Step 3: \(\dfrac{82 - 70}{8} = 1.5\) (IV)
Step 4: Half the area lies above the mean: \(0.5\) (III)
Common mistake: Giving 4 for (A), the mean \(np\), instead of the variance.
Key point: Variance \(= npq\).

questions.sub_topic: Maximum profit with a cubic cost function
questions.question: Revenue is \(R = 50x - x^2\) and cost is \(C = \dfrac{x^3}{3} - 4x^2 + 23x + 30\). The maximum profit is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(213\)
Given: \(P = R - C = -\dfrac{x^3}{3} + 3x^2 + 27x - 30\)
Formula: \(P' = -x^2 + 6x + 27 = -(x - 9)(x + 3) = 0 \Rightarrow x = 9\); \(P''(9) = -12 < 0\)
Step 1: \(P(9) = -243 + 243 + 243 - 30\)
Step 2: \(= 213\)
Common mistake: \(9\) (B) is the output, not the profit. \(243\) (A) forgets the fixed cost of 30.
Key point: Substitute the optimal output into the profit function.

questions.sub_topic: Moving averages and least squares — which claims fail
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) Data for 12 years give 9 centred four-yearly moving averages.
(B) The least squares trend line passes through \((\bar{x}, \bar{y})\).
(C) If the coded \(x\) values add to 0, the intercept \(a\) equals \(\bar{y}\).
(D) Seasonal variation cannot be seen in annual data.
Which of the statements given above is/are NOT correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A) only
Why: Only (A) is false: 12 years give 9 four-yearly averages, and centring pairs of them gives 8.
Why not the others: (B) the normal equations make \(\bar{y} = a + b\bar{x}\). (C) with \(\sum x = 0\), \(a = \dfrac{\sum y}{n}\). (D) seasons repeat within a year, so yearly totals hide them. Options (B), (C) and (D) name a true statement as false.
Key point: Centring a four-yearly series loses one more value.

questions.sub_topic: AB when A² = A and B = I − A
questions.question: \(A\) is a square matrix with \(A^2 = A\), and \(B = I - A\). Then \(AB\) equals:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(O\)
Given: \(B = I - A\)
Formula: \(AB = A(I - A) = A - A^2\)
Step 1: \(A^2 = A\), so \(AB = A - A = O\)
Common mistake: (A) treats \(A^2\) as 0.
Key point: Expand, then use the given identity.

questions.sub_topic: Number of entries in a 3 × 4 matrix
questions.question: The number of entries in a matrix of order \(3 \times 4\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(12\)
Given: 3 rows, 4 columns
Formula: entries \(= m \times n\)
Step 1: \(3 \times 4 = 12\)
Common mistake: \(7\) (A) adds the numbers.
Key point: Each row has one entry for every column.

questions.topic: Unit I: Numbers, Quantification and Numerical Applications
questions.sub_topic: Remainder of 5⁹⁹ on division by 13
questions.question: The remainder when \(5^{99}\) is divided by 13 is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(8\)
Given: \(5^2 = 25 \equiv -1 \pmod{13}\), so \(5^4 \equiv 1\)
Formula: \(5^{99} = (5^4)^{24} \times 5^3\)
Step 1: \(\equiv 5^3 = 125 = 9 \times 13 + 8\)
Step 2: Remainder 8
Common mistake: \(12\) (D) uses \(5^{99} = (5^2)^{49} \times 5\) but reads \((-1)^{49}\) as \(-1 \equiv 12\) and drops the extra 5.
Key point: Find the cycle of powers, then reduce the exponent.

questions.sub_topic: Derivative of e^(3x)
questions.question: \(\dfrac{d}{dx}e^{3x}\) equals:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(3e^{3x}\)
Given: chain rule
Formula: \(\dfrac{d}{dx}e^{ax} = ae^{ax}\)
Step 1: \(3e^{3x}\)
Common mistake: (B) integrates instead.
Key point: Multiply by the derivative of the exponent.

questions.sub_topic: Rate per half-year for 10% compounded half-yearly
questions.question: For a nominal rate of 10% per annum compounded half-yearly, the rate per conversion period is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(5\%\)
Given: 2 conversion periods a year
Formula: \(i = \dfrac{r}{m}\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{10\%}{2} = 5\%\)
Common mistake: \(2.5\%\) (C) is the quarterly rate.
Key point: Divide the nominal rate by the number of periods a year.

questions.sub_topic: Mean of B(40, 0.15)
questions.question: For a binomial distribution with \(n = 40\) and \(p = 0.15\), the mean is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(6\)
Given: \(n = 40\), \(p = 0.15\)
Formula: mean \(= np\)
Step 1: \(40 \times 0.15 = 6\)
Common mistake: \(5.1\) (A) is the variance \(npq\). \(34\) (D) is \(nq\).
Key point: Mean \(= np\).

questions.sub_topic: Least squares trend value for the last of five years
questions.question: Values for 2019–2023 were 10, 13, 15, 18, 19. Coding the years as \(x = -2, \ldots, 2\) and fitting \(y = a + bx\) by least squares, the trend value for 2023 is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(19.6\)
Given: \(\sum y = 75\), \(\sum x^2 = 10\)
Formula: \(a = 15\), \(b = \dfrac{\sum xy}{\sum x^2}\)
Step 1: \(\sum xy = -20 - 13 + 0 + 18 + 38 = 23\), so \(b = 2.3\)
Step 2: 2023 has \(x = 2\): \(15 + 2 \times 2.3 = 19.6\)
Common mistake: \(19\) (A) is the actual value, not the trend value. \(17.3\) (B) uses \(x = 1\).
Key point: The trend value smooths out the actual value.
